chapters.title: Magna Carta
paragraphs: JOHN, King of England by the grace of God, Lord of Ireland, Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and Count of Anjou, sends greetings to his archbishops, bishops, abbots, earls, barons, justices, foresters, sheriffs, stewards, servants, and all his officials and faithful subjects. KNOW THAT, IN GOD’S PRESENCE, we act for the salvation of our soul and the souls of our ancestors and heirs, to honour God, to raise up the holy Church, and to put our kingdom in better order. We do so on the advice of our reverend fathers Stephen, archbishop of Canterbury, primate of all England and cardinal of the holy Roman Church; Henry, archbishop of Dublin; William, bishop of London; Peter, bishop of Winchester; Jocelin, bishop of Bath and Glastonbury; Hugh, bishop of Lincoln; Walter, Bishop of Worcester; William, bishop of Coventry; Benedict, bishop of Rochester; Master Pandulf, subdeacon and member of the papal household; Brother Aymeric, master of the knighthood of the Temple in England; William Marshal, earl of Pembroke; William, earl of Salisbury; William, earl of Warren; William, earl of Arundel; Alan de Galloway, constable of Scotland; Warin Fitz Gerald; Peter Fitz Herbert; Hubert de Burgh, seneschal of Poitou; Hugh de Neville; Matthew Fitz Herbert; Thomas Basset; Alan Basset; Philip Daubeny; Robert de Roppeley; John Marshal; John Fitz Hugh; and other faithful subjects:

(1) FIRST, WE HAVE MADE THIS GRANT TO GOD, and through this charter confirm it for ourselves and our heirs for all time: the English Church is to be free, with none of its rights reduced and none of its liberties impaired. Our wish that this be upheld is shown by what we freely did before the present dispute broke out between us and our barons. We granted and confirmed by charter the Church’s freedom to hold elections—a right considered essential and of the highest importance to it—and obtained confirmation of this from Pope Innocent III. We ourselves will respect this freedom, and we wish our heirs to respect it in good faith for all time.

WE HAVE ALSO GRANTED TO ALL FREE MEN IN OUR KINGDOM, on behalf of ourselves and our heirs for all time, every liberty set down below, to hold and retain from us and our heirs, for themselves and their own heirs:

(2) If an earl, baron, or anyone else holding land directly from the Crown in return for military service dies, and his heir is of full age at his death and owes a ‘relief’, that heir is to receive his inheritance by paying the ‘relief’ at the long-established rate. This means that the heir or heirs of an earl will pay 100 for the earl’s whole barony, and the heir or heirs of a knight will pay no more than 100s. for the knight’s whole ‘fee’. Anyone owing a smaller amount will pay that smaller amount, according to the long-established custom governing ‘fees’.
(3) But if such a person’s heir is a minor under guardianship, he is to receive his inheritance on coming of age without paying either a ‘relief’ or a fine.

(4) A guardian responsible for the land of an heir who is a minor may draw from it only reasonable revenues, customary dues, and feudal services, and must do so without destroying or damaging either people or property. If we entrust the land’s guardianship to a sheriff, or to someone else accountable to us for its revenues, and he causes destruction or damage, we will require him to pay compensation. We will then entrust the land to two worthy, prudent men of the same ‘fee’, accountable for its revenues to us or to the person to whom we have assigned those revenues. If we have granted or sold someone the guardianship of such land and he causes destruction or damage, he will forfeit that guardianship. It will then pass to two worthy, prudent men of the same ‘fee’, who will be accountable to us in the same way.

(5) Throughout his guardianship of such land, the guardian must use the land’s own revenues to keep its houses, parks, fish preserves, ponds, mills, and everything else belonging to it in repair. When the heir reaches full age, the guardian must return the entire property to him, supplied with plough teams and the farming implements needed for that season, to the extent that the land’s revenues can reasonably cover their cost.
(6) Heirs may be married off, but their spouses must not be of lower social standing. The heir’s next-of-kin must be told about the marriage before it takes place.

(7) When her husband dies, a widow is entitled to receive her marriage portion and inheritance immediately and without difficulty. Nothing is to be charged for her dower, her marriage portion, or any inheritance held jointly by her and her husband on the day he died. She is entitled to stay in her husband’s house for forty days following his death, and her dower must be assigned to her during those forty days.

(8) A widow must not be forced to marry while she wishes to live without a husband. She must, however, provide security that she will not remarry without the king’s consent if she holds land from the Crown, or without the consent of the other lord from whom she holds it.

(9) Neither we nor our officials will take land or rent to satisfy a debt while the debtor has enough movable goods to pay it. Nor will we seize the property of his sureties while he himself is able to pay. If he lacks the means to pay the debt, his sureties will become responsible for it. If they wish, they may take possession of his lands and rents until they have been repaid the debt they paid on his behalf, unless the debtor can demonstrate that he has already met his obligations to them.

(10) If someone who has borrowed money from Jews dies before repaying it, his heir will owe no interest on that debt while he is a minor, regardless of the lord from whom he holds his land. If the debt passes to the Crown, the Crown will take only the principal amount recorded in the bond, and nothing more.

(11) If a man dies in debt to Jews, his wife is entitled to her dower without having to use any of it to repay that debt. If he leaves children who are minors, provision may also be made for their needs in proportion to the extent of his landed holding. The debt must be paid from what remains, while preserving the service owed to his feudal lords. The same arrangements are to apply to debts owed to people other than Jews.

(12) No ‘scutage’ or ‘aid’ is to be imposed in our kingdom without its general consent, except to ransom us, to make our eldest son a knight, or, on one occasion only, to marry our eldest daughter. Even for these purposes, the ‘aid’ must be reasonable. The same rules will apply to ‘aids’ levied on the city of London.

(13) The city of London is to retain every ancient liberty and free custom it enjoys, on water as well as on land. We also decree and grant that every other city, borough, town, and port is to retain all its liberties and free customs.

(14) When we seek the realm’s general consent to assess an ‘aid’, other than in the three cases given above, or a ‘scutage’, we will summon the archbishops, bishops, abbots, earls, and greater barons by letters addressed to them individually. Through the sheriffs and other officials, we will issue a general summons to those holding land directly from us, requiring them to gather at a specified place on a specified day, with at least forty days’ notice. Every letter of summons will state why the gathering is being called. Once the summons has been issued, the business set for that day will proceed according to the decision of those who attend, even if some of those summoned have failed to appear.

(15) From now on, we will permit no one to impose an ‘aid’ on his free men except to ransom himself, to make his eldest son a knight, or, on one occasion only, to marry his eldest daughter. The ‘aid’ imposed for these purposes must be reasonable.
(16) No man is to be compelled to provide more service for a knight’s ‘fee’, or for any other free holding of land, than that holding requires.
(17) Ordinary lawsuits are to be heard at a settled location, rather than moving from place to place with the royal court.

(18) Inquests of novel disseisin, mort d’ancestor, and darrein presentment must be heard only in the county court to which they belong. Four times each year we will send two justices to every county; if we are abroad, our chief justice will send them. Alongside four knights chosen by that county, these justices will conduct the assizes in the county court, at the place and on the day when that court meets.

(19) If some assizes cannot be heard on the day the county court meets, enough of the knights and freeholders attending must stay behind afterwards to ensure that justice is administered, taking into account the amount of business still to be completed.

(20) A free man who commits a minor offence is to be fined only in proportion to that offence; a serious offence is to receive a proportionate fine too, but never one so heavy that it takes away his livelihood. Likewise, when a merchant or a husbandman falls at the mercy of a royal court, the merchant must retain his merchandise and the husbandman his farming implements. No such fine may be imposed unless reputable men from the neighbourhood have assessed it under oath.
(21) Only their equals may fine earls and barons, and the amount must correspond to the seriousness of the offence they have committed.
(22) When a clerk in holy orders is fined on his lay property, the fine must be assessed by these same principles, without taking the value of his ecclesiastical benefice into account.
(23) No town or individual may be compelled to build a bridge across a river unless an ancient obligation requires them to do so.
(24) Sheriffs, constables, coroners, and other royal officials must not hear lawsuits that fall within the jurisdiction of the royal justices.
(25) The rent of every county, hundred, wapentake, and tithing must stay at its long-established level and must not rise; royal demesne manors are the exception.

(26) If a man holding a lay ‘fee’ from the Crown dies, and a sheriff or royal official presents royal letters patent summoning payment of a debt owed to the Crown, those officials may lawfully seize and make an inventory of movable goods found in the deceased’s lay ‘fee’. They may do so up to the value of the debt, as assessed by worthy men. Nothing may be taken away before the entire debt has been paid. Once it is paid, the remainder must pass to the executors so they can carry out the deceased’s will. If he owes the Crown nothing, all his movable goods must be treated as his property, apart from the reasonable shares belonging to his wife and children.

(27) If a free man dies intestate, leaving no will, his next-of-kin and friends must distribute his movable goods under the Church’s supervision. The rights of those who owe him debts must remain protected.
(28) No constable or other royal official may take a man’s corn or other movable goods without paying for them immediately, unless the seller freely agrees to accept payment later.

(29) A constable must not force a knight to pay money for castle-guard if the knight is prepared to serve as guard himself, or, if he has a reasonable excuse, to provide another suitable man to serve instead. A knight taken or sent away on military service is to be released from castle-guard for as long as that service lasts.
(30) No sheriff, royal official, or anyone else may take a free man’s horses or carts to use for transport unless he agrees to it.
(31) Neither we nor any of our royal officials will take timber for our castle, or for any other use, unless its owner gives consent.
(32) We will retain the lands of those convicted of felony for no more than one year and one day. Once that time has passed, the lands must be given back to the lords of the relevant ‘fees’.
(33) Every fish-weir in the Thames and the Medway must be taken away, as must those elsewhere throughout England, with the exception of those on the sea coast.
(34) From now on, no one may receive the writ known as precipe concerning a holding of land if its issue could take away a free man’s right to have his case tried in his own lord’s court.

(35) Measures for wine, ale, and corn must be uniform across the kingdom, with the London quarter used for corn. Dyed cloth, russett, and haberject must also have a uniform width: two ells measured inside the selvedges. The same principle of uniform standards must apply to weights.
(36) From now on, no payment is to be made or received for issuing a writ of inquisition of life or limbs. Such a writ must be supplied free of charge and must not be withheld.

(37) If a man holds land from the Crown by ‘fee-farm’, ‘socage’, or ‘burgage’, while also holding land from another lord in return for knight’s service, those ‘fee-farm’, ‘socage’, or ‘burgage’ holdings will not entitle us to guardianship of his heir or of the land within the other lord’s ‘fee’, unless the ‘fee-farm’ itself owes knight’s service. Nor will we claim guardianship of a man’s heir, or of land he holds from someone else, because he holds a small property from the Crown in return for supplying knives, arrows, or a similar service.
(38) From now on, no official may put a man on trial on the strength of that official’s unsupported word alone. He must produce trustworthy witnesses who can confirm his statement.

(39) No free man may be arrested or imprisoned, deprived of his rights or property, declared an outlaw, sent into exile, or lose his standing in any other way unless this follows a lawful judgement by his equals or the law of the land. Nor will we use force against him, or send others to use it, except on those same grounds.
(40) We will sell right or justice to no one, and we will refuse or delay it for no one.

(41) Every merchant may come into England or leave it safely and without fear, and may remain here or travel by land or water to trade, without unlawful charges, in keeping with ancient lawful customs. In wartime, however, this does not apply to merchants from a country at war with us. If such merchants are in our country when war begins, they must be detained, but neither they nor their property may be harmed, until we or our chief justice have established how our merchants are being treated in the enemy country. If our merchants are kept safe there, those merchants will be kept safe here as well.

(42) From now on, any man may lawfully leave our kingdom and return by land or water safely and without fear, provided he maintains his allegiance to us. In wartime, this freedom may be suspended briefly for the realm’s common benefit. This provision does not apply to those imprisoned or outlawed under the law of the land, to people from a country at war with us, or to merchants, whose treatment is set out above.

(43) If a man holds lands belonging to an ‘escheat’, such as the ‘honour’ of Wallingford, Nottingham, Boulogne, or Lancaster, or another ‘escheat’ in our possession that is a barony, his heir, on his death, will owe us only the ‘relief’ and service that he would have owed the baron if the baron still possessed the barony. We will hold that ‘escheat’ on the same terms on which the baron held it.

(44) From now on, those who live outside the forest will not have to attend the royal forest justices in response to a general summons, unless they are directly involved in the proceedings or have acted as sureties for someone arrested for an offence concerning the forest.
(45) We will choose as justices, constables, sheriffs, and other officials only men who understand the kingdom’s law and intend to uphold it properly.

(46) Every baron who has founded an abbey, and can prove this through a charter of an English king or through ancient tenure, may exercise guardianship over it while it has no abbot, as his right allows.
(47) Every forest established during our reign must immediately be disafforested, losing its forest status. River-banks enclosed during our reign must likewise be freed from those enclosures.

(48) In every county, twelve knights of that county, acting under oath, must immediately investigate all evil customs concerning forests and warrens, foresters and warreners, sheriffs and their servants, and river-banks and their wardens. Within forty days of their investigation, those evil customs must be ended completely and permanently. Before this is done, however, we must be informed, or, if we are outside England, our chief justice must be informed.

(49) We will immediately give back all hostages and charters that Englishmen have handed over to us as guarantees of peace or faithful service. (50) We will dismiss from office entirely the kinsmen of Gerard de Ath, Peter, Guy, and Andrew de Chanceaux, and Guy de Cigogne; they are to hold no office in England from now on. Those concerned are Engelard de Cigogn, Geoffrey de Martigny and his brothers, Philip Marc and his brothers, together with Geoffrey his nephew and all their followers.
As soon as peace has returned, we will expel from the kingdom all foreign knights, bowmen, their attendants, and mercenaries who have entered it with horses and weapons and brought it harm.

If we have taken a man’s lands, castles, liberties, or rights from him, or dispossessed him of them, without a lawful judgement by his equals, we will restore them immediately. Any dispute will be settled by the judgement of the twenty-five barons named below in the clause that guarantees the peace. But if our father King Henry or our brother King Richard deprived or dispossessed a man of something without such a judgement, and we still hold it or others hold it under our warranty, we will have the delay usually granted to Crusaders. This delay will not apply if a lawsuit had already begun, or an enquiry had already been ordered by us, before we took the Cross as a Crusader. Once we return from the Crusade, or if we give it up, we will immediately provide full justice.

We will have the same delay in providing justice over forests that are to be disafforested or to retain forest status, where our father Henry or our brother Richard first afforested them; over guardianship of lands in someone else’s fee, where we have previously exercised that guardianship because a third party held a fee from us for knight’s service; and over abbeys founded in someone else’s fee, where the lord of that fee claims a right. When we return from the Crusade, or if we give it up, we will immediately provide full justice in response to complaints concerning these matters.
No one may be arrested or sent to prison on a woman’s appeal concerning someone’s death, unless the person who died was her husband.

Every fine paid to us unjustly and contrary to the law of the land, and every fine we have unjustly demanded, must be cancelled in full, or the matter must be settled by a majority judgement of the twenty-five barons named below in the clause guaranteeing the peace. Stephen, archbishop of Canterbury, will join them if he can attend, along with anyone else he wishes to bring. If the archbishop cannot attend, the proceedings will go ahead without him. If, however, any of those twenty-five barons has himself been involved in a similar lawsuit, his judgement must be excluded. The other members of the twenty-five must choose and swear in someone else to replace him for that occasion alone.

If we have taken lands, liberties, or anything else from Welshmen in England or Wales, or dispossessed them of these things, without a lawful judgement by their equals, they must receive them back immediately. Any dispute about this must be settled in the Marches by a judgement of equals. Land held in England will be governed by English law, land in Wales by Welsh law, and land in the Marches by the law of the Marches. The Welsh must treat us and our people in the same manner.

If our father King Henry or our brother King Richard deprived or dispossessed a Welshman of anything without a lawful judgement by his equals, and we still hold it or others hold it under our warranty, we will have the delay usually granted to Crusaders. This will not apply if a lawsuit had already begun, or an enquiry had been ordered by us, before we took the Cross as a Crusader. But when we return from the Crusade, or if we give it up, we will immediately provide full justice under the laws of Wales and the regions just mentioned.
We will immediately give back Llywelyn’s son, every Welsh hostage, and the charters handed over to us as guarantees that peace would be kept.

In returning the sisters and hostages of Alexander, king of Scotland, and restoring his liberties and rights, we will treat him as we treat our other barons in England. An exception will apply only if the charters we hold from his father William, the former king of Scotland, show that a different treatment is required. His equals in our court will decide the matter by their judgement.

All the customs and liberties we have granted here must be respected throughout our kingdom in our dealings with our subjects. Every man in our kingdom, whether a member of the clergy or a layman, must likewise respect them in his dealings with his own men.

WE HAVE GRANTED ALL THESE THINGS for God, to put our kingdom in better order, and to settle the discord that has arisen between us and our barons. Since we wish all these grants to be enjoyed fully and to remain firmly in force for ever, we give the barons the following guarantee:
The barons must choose twenty-five from among themselves to uphold, and to use all their power to ensure respect for, the peace and liberties granted and confirmed to them in this charter.

If we, our chief justice, any of our officials, or any of our servants wrong any man in any way, or break any article of the peace or of this guarantee, and four of the twenty-five barons are informed of the offence, those four must come to us—or, if we are outside the kingdom, to the chief justice—to report it and demand immediate redress. If we, or the chief justice while we are abroad, fail to provide redress within forty days from the day the offence was reported to us or to him, the four barons must take the matter to the rest of the twenty-five. With the support of the whole community of the land, they may distrain upon us and attack us in every possible way, taking our castles, lands, possessions, or anything else, until they obtain the redress they have decided upon. Only our own person and the persons of the queen and our children are exempt. Once they have obtained that redress, they may return to their usual obedience to us.

Any man who wishes may swear an oath to carry out the commands of the twenty-five barons in pursuit of these ends, and to join them in attacking us with all the power he has. We openly and freely permit anyone who wishes to take this oath to do so, and we will never forbid anyone to take it. Indeed, if any of our subjects are unwilling to take the oath, we will command them to swear it and compel them to obey.

If any of the twenty-five barons dies, leaves the country, or is otherwise unable to carry out his duties, the remaining barons must select another baron to replace him, according to their judgement. He must then be sworn in just as they were.

If the twenty-five barons disagree about a matter submitted to them for decision, the judgement of a majority of those attending will be as valid as a unanimous judgement of all twenty-five. This holds whether all are present or whether some of those summoned are unwilling or unable to attend.
The twenty-five barons must take an oath to uphold every article above faithfully, and must do all within their power to ensure that others uphold them too.

We will not try, either ourselves or through anyone acting for us, to obtain from anyone anything that could cancel or reduce any part of these grants or liberties. If anything of that kind is obtained, it will have no legal force, and we will never make use of it, whether directly or through anyone acting for us.

We have completely forgiven and pardoned everyone for all ill-will, injuries, or grudges arising between us and our subjects, clergy or laymen, from the beginning of this dispute. We have also fully remitted, and for our own part pardoned, all offences by clergy or laymen committed as a consequence of that dispute between Easter 1215 AD and the return of peace.

We have also had letters patent drawn up for the barons to attest to this guarantee and the grants set out above. These bear the seals of Stephen, archbishop of Canterbury, Henry, archbishop of Dublin, the other bishops named above, and Master Pandulf.

WE THEREFORE WISH AND COMMAND that the English Church remain free, and that the men of our kingdom possess and retain every one of these liberties, rights, and grants, fully, entirely, and in peace, for themselves and their heirs, holding them from us and our heirs, in every matter and every place, for all time.
We and the barons have both sworn to uphold all of this honestly and in good faith, without deception. Those named above and many others stand as witnesses.
Issued by our own hand in the meadow known as Runnymede, between Windsor and Staines, on the fifteenth day of June, in the seventeenth year of our reign.
